text: While all those changes mean struggling banks, auto companies facing possible bankruptcy and all that government spending. That may sound like a disaster to you but some people hear the sweet sound of opportunity. Reporter Chana Joffe-Walt explains.

Barry Silbert is a Wall Street guide. He runs a Wall Street company, and he's got problems. His windows are just a little too big, that view of the Statue of Liberty a little too distracting. And when he looks over at his enormous new desk from across his enormous new office, he thinks, man, I really need to decorate.
Definitely needed something for the wall, nice picture or something. Picture of my wife, I got to put that up. And.
Plants?
Plants would be good, right?

Silbert runs a financial company called SecondMarket, and it's growing like crazy. He doesn't have time to decorate these days because, well, this may sound painful to hear if you work at a financial firm or a retail operation or a non-profit, or pretty much anywhere but here, but Silbert can't hire people fast enough.

We're hiring designers and developers with a technology background. We're hiring people with marketing backgrounds, research backgrounds. We're hiring quite frankly in all aspects or all areas of organization.

So why is this financial firm skipping along while all its neighbors are tripping, scraping knees and then getting run over by a bus? When Congress authorized Treasury to spend $700 billion on toxic assets, people asked questions. How will it work? Where was the infrastructure? How will all that stuff get priced? And at the same time, the question in Barry Silbert's mind, how can we get in on this? His answer was a marketplace for toxic waste. If no one knows what all these stuff is worth, create a place where it's all for sale and buyers can bid on it, and then you'll find out. Sort of like a consignment store, right. Each person has all the stuff in their attic. And when it's up there in the attic it's junk, but drag it to the consignment store and maybe it's not anymore. If the government was going to be buying toxic assets from someone, Silbert wanted it to be him.
So our focus over the past few months has been preparing to expand SecondMarket into those assets that the government was planning to buy.

A funny thing happened while Silbert was following the government's lead to toxic waste. The government changed direction. I met Silbert on Tuesday, on Wednesday, Secretary Paulson announced the bailout money would not actually be used to buy up toxic assets. And on Thursday, yesterday, I had to go back to Silbert.
So you still didn't put up the picture of your wife yet?
Oh, you know, I was right there. It was up - it was up all along, right there.
Silbert sits down on one of his shiny leather chairs and considers this new world he faces.
The government had a lot of money to put to work. And so now we are completely dependent or reliant on private capital to establish the prices.

The entire premise of the government bailout was that no one from the private sector wanted this stuff ,and the people who owned it? They weren't about to give it away for close to nothing. So, here's Silbert. He's got his downtown office, the software, the staff, he's totally ready to trade toxic assets. But his biggest potential buyer has just disappeared. But Silbert says that may not actually matter. He says many of his 1,500 clients, especially the hedge funds, they're calling him up telling him, government or not, they want in.
There's a whole group of buyers of this type of thing, but it's probably either six, nine, 12 months before we see sufficient number of buyers to really start propping up the prices.
So you're not worried that there are going to be people who are going to be willing to sell these assets or people that are willing to buy them?
Absolutely not. I'm not worried about that.

If Silbert is right to sleep so soundly, it could mean that he was even more enterprising than he meant to be, accidentally building a company that could have a lock on the toxic waste market, for whatever that's worth. For NPR News, I'm Chana Joffe-Walt in New York.

Around 20 years ago, Americans began shifting the way we think about our homes and the mortgages used to finance them. To take note of this change, we sent Planet Money's Chana Joffe-Walt on a mission.
This all started because my editor used to watch "All in the Family" as a kid.
Well, not just because of that.
And there he is - Steve Drummond, NPR's national editor. It was, right? Because you remember watching Archie Bunker burn his mortgage.

That certainly is part of it. But I was also - throughout this crisis, I've been thinking about the idea of a 30-year mortgage and how crazy that seems to me now. I'll be 76 or so when I pay mine off, and I don't even really think about it as a real possibility. But people do pay off their mortgages - like you used to hear about people burning the mortgage.
Like Archie Bunker.
Exactly.
(as Archie Bunker) Burning the mortgage over here.
(as Edith Bunker) Archie, be careful. Don't set fire to the house. Remember Cousin Henry.
(As Archie Bunker) Yeah, I always hated him.

Anyway, so, yeah. I thought it would be cool to meet someone like that. We keep hearing about tens of thousands of people losing their homes, and I wanted to hear from somebody who had actually paid off a 30-year mortgage. And Chana, you said you were going to do a story.
I'm in search of people who are towards the end of paying off a 30-year mortgage.
Good luck.
Why do you say good luck?
Oh, well, there's been multiple times over last 15 years where interest rates have dipped down and people have refinanced. And typically what happened, for the most part, reset the clock.
So, what? This one guy didn't know anyone?
Yeah, I know what you're thinking. I called lots and lots of other people, mortgage brokers, banks, community lending people - the whole shebang, Steve.
One time in the last 28 years, I have seen a title report...
Towards the end of this 30-year-mortgage, you might be looking for an endangered species.
There's one couple that I know that may have done that, but I'm not sure that they paid it off. Yeah, actually they won the lotto.
No way, really?
Yeah.
Steve, that was Judy Holser, Erica Malone, and Robin Finley, all veteran mortgage business people laughing at me.
So, Chana, you did - this all just to tell me you didn't do this story?
No, Steve. Come on. I've got you.
Come in, come in.
Hello.
(unintelligible) is not here yet.
Welcome to the home of Tamar and Chris Piersal in Seattle. These two bought a home in 1978, paid it off 28 years later.
Hey, you found it.
Yeah, they were great. So Chris rides his motorcycle everywhere, and Tamar is in IT, and she's got this great laugh.
They're one of those couples that's been together so long, they talk in this way, like, their sentences are made up of parts from one of them and parts from the other.
It was just...
...a day to day thing...
...a payment that we made every month.
Well, you know, I think there was a point when we started...
...we could see...
...it's not a never-never kind of thing so...

We could see that - yeah, and that was exciting, the idea that we wouldn't have to make that payment every month. We suddenly were kind of electrified by the notion that we could own this free and clear.

So here's the thing about this assignment, Steve, why I think the Piersals were so hard to find: So first of all, there are just fewer people like them. Just in the last 10 years, there's been a seven percent decline in people who own their own homes free and clear of debt. But that still leaves us with a lot of people, something like 30 percent of home owners don't have any mortgage debt. But those people tend to be older, older than the Piersals, and just of a generation that was really uncomfortable with the idea of debt.
Yeah, but as interest rates went down, millions of people refinanced, and that wasn't necessarily bad. Lots of people saved, you know, a lot of money on their monthly payments.

True. It just didn't always used to be like that. Tamar basically says, look, we never refinanced. We just made the payments. And Chris says he thought about moving once or twice, but he'd look around at those houses for sale and the prices.
You know, for us, when they started talking houses in sub increments of a million dollars, we're going, huh? That's a lot of money.
Yeah, an ordinary house for half a million or $700,000, it sounded outlandish.
Uh-oh. I don't want to know.
Thirty-five thousand, Steve, the Piersal's house, 1976, cost $35,000.
Ouch. That hurts my brain. Okay. So the real question here: Was there a mortgage burning involved?
Sorry.

Well, I remember when we made the last payment. I was at work, and I was on the phone with the mortgage company, and my co-workers were all going, oh, we've never known anyone who paid off their mortgage.
They were all standing around.
I'd always heard of people burning the mortgage.
Yeah.
But there was nothing to burn.
I think we out to dinner.
Yeah, we went out to dinner.
Yeah.
Yeah, that's what we did.

The Piersal's son actually just became a homeowner, too. He got a home that was in foreclosure. And he says he will be there 30 years, till he owns the place, at which point, Steve, he promises he will burn something. You happy?
Yes, very happy.
Okay. Chana Joffe-Walt, NPR News, Seattle.
